title: Heeney Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Heeney wells have a 135 ft median depth, with fractured-bedrock drilling commonly costing $14,800-$25,500 finished.
h1: What Heeney Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Buying land near Heeney means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well records, and site conditions that can change from one lot to the next. Within 5 miles of Heeney, Colorado, DWR records show 236 permitted wells. Of those, 137 are recorded as constructed, 150 report a total depth, 56 report a pump yield, and 20 report a static water level.

The records are useful for setting expectations, but they are not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. A neighboring well can show the likely geology and cost range, while a site evaluation, permit review, and experienced driller help determine what your parcel can actually support.

sections.heading: Heeney Well Depths Reflect Fractured Mountain Rock
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Heeney is 135 feet. The middle half runs from 76 to 232 feet, which is a practical range to carry into an early drilling estimate. About 35% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 47% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 13% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 5% reach 600 feet or more.

The deepest well on record is 1,075 feet. That outlier matters because Heeney wells commonly draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers: 227 permits identify that setting. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures rather than a uniform, predictable layer, so depth and production can change substantially across short distances.

sections.heading: Most Heeney Wells Produce a Usable Household Yield
sections.html:
Among the 56 Heeney-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. That is a generally workable range for a household well when the pressure system, storage, and building demand are designed correctly.

Yield is not evenly distributed. Seventy percent of reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 12% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Four percent are under 1 gallon per minute, and 14% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A buyer should not treat the median as a promise. Ask for the completion report, pump test information, and any storage-tank plans before relying on a well for a home.

sections.heading: Heeney Water Levels Are Recorded Sparingly
sections.html:
Only 20 wells in the local records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. In those records, the median depth to static water is 90 feet, with the middle half between 40 and 130 feet. That helps with pump planning, but it does not establish the water level on every parcel.

The permit totals by decade do not show a water-table trend. They show when permits were issued, not how water levels changed over time. A recent permit year is 2025, and the records include permits from the 1950s through the 2020s. For a specific property, compare nearby completion reports and ask whether the well has a documented static level after it has rested.

sections.heading: Permit History Shows Long Use Around Heeney
sections.html:
Heeney has a long record of domestic well development. The permit counts by decade are 2 in the 1950s, 15 in the 1960s, 21 in the 1970s, 40 in the 1980s, 49 in the 1990s, 37 in the 2000s, 15 in the 2010s, and 21 in the 2020s. Most permits are for domestic or household use, which accounts for 81% of the use mix.

The most active drillers in these records are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 40 permits; Buena Vista Drilling, associated with Shelton, William L, with 23; and Arrow Drilling, associated with Berglund, Peter R., with 19. Those records can help identify local experience, but confirm current licensing, availability, and scope directly.

sections.heading: A Heeney Well Can Cost More Than the Hole
sections.html:
Heeney ground is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling cost model uses a typical rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 135 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $8,800 to $13,500.

A finished well is a larger project. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled total is about $14,800 to $25,500. That range is for the median-depth scenario, not a fixed bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, a low-yield well requiring storage, and long utility runs can change the price. Get the drilling scope in writing and ask what happens if the first target does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Yield, and the Building Site
sections.html:
Environmental history deserves a specific review before buying. Within about 10 miles of Heeney, mapped records include 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 13 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These findings do not prove a private well is contaminated, but they support testing for site-appropriate contaminants and reviewing nearby land uses.

Low yield and dry holes are also real risks in fractured rock. Confirm the well location, access for a rig, expected casing and grout, and the separation between the well, septic system, and proposed building. The permit’s use matters too: 81% are domestic or household wells, while other permits serve stock, irrigation, or monitoring uses. Before construction, verify the DWR permit, septic approval, and any water-right or augmentation requirements that apply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Heeney?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Heeney is 135 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 76 to 232 feet. About 35% are under 100 feet, and 47% are between 100 and 300 feet. Depth is less predictable in fractured granite and gneiss; the deepest recorded well reaches 1,075 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Heeney?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 135-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,800 to $13,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at $14,800 to $25,500. A deeper hole, difficult access, or low yield can increase the final cost.

faq.q: How much water do Heeney wells produce?
faq.a: Among 56 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half produces 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Four percent report under 1 gallon per minute, so buyers should review the actual pump test rather than rely only on the median.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Heeney?
faq.a: A private well must be evaluated and tested at the property. Mapped records within about 10 miles include 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 13 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those records do not establish contamination in a particular well, but they make water-quality testing and a site-history review important.

faq.q: Are Heeney wells getting deeper or running lower?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a dropping water table. Only 20 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 90 feet and a middle half from 40 to 130 feet. Permit counts by decade describe permit timing, not water-level change. For a property decision, compare nearby completion reports and obtain current well information.
